P3'.answer:
The weakest point is the thing you're proudest of, and it's not the phone-only principle itself — it's that phone-only collides head-on with "I work alone, 8 to 6, hands in a bike all day."

Think through what actually happens. A customer rings at 11am. You're elbow-deep in a bottom bracket at someone's house. You either:

- stop, wipe your hands, answer, and lose five minutes plus your flow on every call (and the customer in front of you watches you take other people's calls), or
- let it ring to voicemail — in which case your "talk to a real person" promise has just delivered the customer to a machine, which is the exact thing you built the policy to avoid.

Then you ring back at 6:30pm, they don't pick up, and you're playing phone tag for a £40 job. Multiply that by 300 regulars plus walk-ins, and a meaningful chunk of your bookings will leak away — not because people dislike phoning, but because nobody can reach you. The people most likely to give up are the new customers you don't have a relationship with yet, which is exactly where growth comes from.

The rest of the plan is genuinely solid: qualified, equipped, insured, inherited customer base, low overhead. The one structural gap is that you have a one-person business with a booking channel that requires a person to be free during working hours, and that person isn't free.

Ways to keep the heart of the idea without the hole:

- **Keep phone as the primary channel, but add a safety net** — a simple text or online form saying "request a callback," so a missed call isn't a lost customer. You still call everyone back personally; you've just caught them first.
- **A proper voicemail that sets a promise** — "I'm mid-repair, I'll ring you back before 7 tonight" — and then actually do it, every day, as a fixed 30-minute block.
- **Part-time phone cover** — a partner, a retired mate, a call-answering service for a few quid a day. "Every customer talks to a real person" doesn't have to mean *you*.
- **Track missed calls for the first month.** If you're missing 20+ a week, you'll have your answer in data rather than my opinion.

You can absolutely keep the human-contact principle. Just don't let the booking channel depend on the one person who's never available to pick up.

P3'.answer:
The weakest point is the one you're proudest of, and it's not the idea itself — it's the collision between phone-only bookings and working alone with your hands in a bike from 8 to 6.

Think about what a booking call actually looks like from your side: you're mid-job, hands greasy, maybe halfway through bleeding a brake. The phone rings. You either stop (cost: time, a half-finished job, grease on the phone, a customer in front of you watching you take another customer's call) or you let it go to voicemail. Most people won't leave a voicemail, and many won't call back — they'll ring the next mechanic on the list, or go back to a shop with a website. Your 300 inherited regulars will tolerate this for a while because they know you. New customers won't. So your main acquisition channel is also your biggest leak.

The rest of the plan is solid — qualified, tooled up, insured, a ready-made customer base. That's why this is the thing worth fixing before launch, not after.

The good news is you don't have to abandon the principle. "Every customer talks to a real person" is a fine idea; "every customer talks to *me, live, whenever they call*" is the version that doesn't work. Options:

- **Set a call-back promise instead of a live-answer promise.** Voicemail greeting says "I'm under a bike, leave your name and number and I'll call back by 1pm / 6pm." Then actually do it, every day, at fixed times. People accept this from tradespeople.
- **Allow text/WhatsApp for first contact**, then you call them back. It's still a person-to-person conversation, just not at the moment they happen to ring.
- **Pay for a part-time answering service or a local person** (a few hours a day) to take calls and book slots in a shared calendar. Cheap relative to lost jobs.
- **Block an hour a day for the phone** and tell customers that's when you're reachable live.

One more thing, smaller: being phone-only also means being findable-only-by-word-of-mouth. You don't need an app, but a one-page Google Business listing with your number and hours costs nothing and is how people will find your phone number in the first place.

P3'.answer:
The weakest point is the phone-only booking combined with working alone.

You'll be under a bike or in a customer's driveway from 8 to 6, so you'll miss most calls. A missed call from someone who has never used you usually becomes a booking for a competitor, because people rarely leave voicemails or call back. Your 300 regulars will probably put up with it, but new customers, who you need for growth, are the ones most likely to drop out.

Some facts that bear on it:
- Many people, especially under 40, prefer to book online or by text, and some will not phone at all.
- Calls taken while working are interrupted, and you'll be fielding them with greasy hands, in noise, without your diary in front of you.
- Without a website, you are largely invisible in local searches ("bike repair near me") and on Google Maps, which is a main source of new mobile-service customers.

You can keep the idea of talking to a real person without losing bookings:
- Set aside fixed call-back windows (e.g. 8-8:30 and 6-7pm) and say so in your voicemail message.
- Offer text or WhatsApp as a way to request a call, and still have the conversation by phone.
- Set up a free Google Business Profile with your number and hours, and a simple one-page site with a "request a call back" form. This is not an online booking system, and it still ends in a conversation.

Secondary risks: no cover when you're ill or on holiday, and travel time between jobs reducing the number of billable hours per day.

The phone-only booking — the part you're proudest of.

Not the idea behind it. "Every customer talks to a real person" is a genuine selling point, especially against app-based competitors. The problem is the mechanics: you're the only person, and from 8 to 6 your hands are inside a bike. So who answers the phone?

Either you stop every job to take calls — greasy hands, half-stripped bottom bracket, customer standing there while you book someone else — or you let it ring and the call goes to voicemail. Most people who get voicemail from a tradesperson don't leave a message; they try the next number. You've got 300 regulars handed to you, which is a real asset, but every one of those people who rings and gets nothing is a quiet leak, and you'll never see it happen.

The fix doesn't mean abandoning the principle. It means separating "a real person talks to every customer" from "I personally answer live calls all day." Options, roughly in order of cost:

- A voicemail greeting that says exactly when you'll call back ("I'm on a job — I return every call between 12:30 and 1 and after 6") and then actually doing it, religiously.
- A simple text or web form that captures name, number, and problem, and *you ring them back*. They still talk to a real person — you just control when.
- Later, a few hours a day of someone answering for you (a family member, a virtual receptionist).

Everything else in the plan is solid: qualified, equipped, insured, with an inherited customer base. That's a better start than most. But the booking method as currently designed is the one piece that works against the man doing the work.

The weakest point is phone-only booking combined with working alone, out on jobs, with your hands in a bike from 8 to 6. Those two choices work against each other.

- **You can't answer the phone during the hours people call.** Most people ring during the working day, usually on a break, and if you don't pick up, many won't leave a voicemail. They'll search for the next repairer who responds. Every missed call is a lost job, and as a new business you can't afford that.
- **Answering mid-job costs you too.** Stopping to take calls breaks your concentration, slows the repair, and can sound rushed or distracted on the customer's end, which undercuts the "real person" experience you want.
- **Some customers will never phone.** Many people, especially under 40, will text or book online rather than call. You'd be turning away part of your market for the sake of a principle.

Your 300 regulars will probably ring you, so the problem won't show up straight away. It will show up when you try to grow beyond them.

You can keep the heart of the idea, which is that a real person is involved, without making the phone the only door:

1. **Set callback windows.** Have a voicemail say, "I'm out on a job, I return calls at 12:30 and 5:30." People accept this from a tradesperson.
2. **Accept texts or WhatsApp** as well as calls, so people can reach you in a few seconds and you can reply between jobs.
3. **Add a one-page website** with your number, your area, your prices, and a "request a callback" form. It can say you'll phone everyone personally to confirm. That keeps the human contact and fixes discoverability.

A few smaller risks are worth checking. Travel time between jobs cuts into billable hours, so your pricing should account for it. And as a solo operator, illness or a van breakdown stops all income. Neither is as serious as the phone issue.

You've done the hard parts well: the skills, the van, the insurance, and a ready customer base. The booking method is the one decision that could undermine them, and it's cheap to fix.

The rest of the plan is strong: real experience, equipment paid for, insurance sorted, and 300 existing customers on day one, which most new businesses never get. But your booking system relies on you answering the phone at exactly the hours you're least able to. In practice:

1. **Set call windows.** For example, 7:30–8:00, 12:30–1:00 and 6:00–6:30, stated clearly on your voicemail and van. People accept "I'll call you back at lunchtime" if they know it's coming.
2. **Use a good voicemail message** that promises a callback the same day and keeps that promise.
3. **Consider a call-answering service** (around £50–150/month in the UK). A real human answers, takes details, and you call back to confirm. Customers still talk to a person.
4. **Get a free Google Business Profile.** It isn't online booking. It just shows your phone number, area and reviews to people searching. This alone solves most of the discoverability problem.
5. **Text confirmations**, sent after the call, cut no-shows without replacing the conversation.

2. **Accept texts or WhatsApp.** It's still you replying, just on your schedule. Many customers will prefer it, and you can send photos or quotes easily.
3. **Use an answering service** (around £30–80/month in the UK). A real person takes the details and you call back. This fits your "talk to a real person" value.
4. **Even a one-page website** with your number, area, prices, and call-back times helps new customers find and trust you, without any online booking.

**Act on this early.** The 300 handed-over regulars are your biggest asset, but they're used to walking into a shop. The weakest point is the phone-only booking, and it's tied to your working pattern.

You'll be alone, under a bike, from 8 to 6. You can't answer a call with your hands in a drivetrain, so most calls will go to voicemail. People who ring a tradesperson and get no answer usually ring the next name on the list, and new customers (beyond your 300 regulars) will do this most. The one thing meant to set you apart becomes the thing that loses you work, because the "real person" is mostly unavailable during the hours people call.

Some other consequences:

- **Constant interruptions.** Stopping mid-job to take calls slows you down and can annoy the customer whose bike you're working on. Not stopping means missed bookings.
- **Evening admin.** You'd be returning calls after 6, when you're tired, and customers may have already booked elsewhere.
- **Discovery.** Most people find local services by searching online. With no website, you're invisible to anyone who isn't already one of your regulars. A Google Business Profile alone, with your number, reviews and service area, would cost nothing and help a lot.
- **Growth.** Your regulars may keep you busy at first, but customers drift away, and you'll need new ones.

You don't have to give up the personal touch. Keep phone as the main way to book, but protect it:

1. Set aside fixed call windows, say 7:30-8:00, lunch, and 6:00-6:30, and say so in your voicemail.
2. Have a clear voicemail promising a call back within a set time.
3. Add a simple web presence: a Google Business Profile and a one-page site with your number, prices, area and hours. That's information, not online booking, so it doesn't compromise your principle.
4. Consider a text or WhatsApp number as a secondary route. Many people prefer it, and you can reply between jobs.
5. If it gets busy, a part-time call-answering service or a helper for a few hours a week would keep the human voice without you dropping tools.

The rest of your plan is strong: skills, insurance, equipment and a ready customer base. The risk is mainly in how people reach you, and that's cheap to fix before you've lost customers rather than after.

P3'.answer:
The weakest point is the one you're proudest of. **Phone-only booking doesn't fit a schedule where you're alone with your hands in a bike from 8 to 6.**

**Why it's the weak spot**

- **You'll miss most calls.** You can't answer with greasy hands, mid-repair, under a van, or while driving. Stopping a job for every call slows the work you're paid for.
- **Missed calls cost you customers.** Many people who reach voicemail don't leave a message. They ring the next name on Google. For a new business, a missed call is often a lost job.
- **The real-person promise can backfire.** You want everyone to talk to a human, but if callers usually get voicemail, they talk to no one. Ringing back at 7pm is phone tag, not personal service.
- **It limits your 300 inherited regulars.** They're your best asset, but they were used to walking into a shop. Some will try once, fail to reach you, and drift elsewhere. The handover period is when you can least afford that.
- **Evenings vanish.** Callbacks, rescheduling and directions all land after 6pm, on top of invoicing and parts orders.

**How to keep the heart of the idea and fix it**

- **Set call hours.** For example, 8–8:30am, 12:30–1pm and 5:30–6pm. Put them on your voicemail, van and cards: "I answer live at these times; otherwise I'll call you back the same day." People accept limits when they know what to expect.
- **Use a voicemail that works for you.** Ask for name, location, the bike problem and a good callback time, and promise a callback window.
- **Add a "request a call" form.** This isn't online booking. Customers leave details and you phone them. Every customer still talks to you, but on your schedule, and you don't lose the people who won't leave voicemail.
- **Text the regulars now.** You have 300 warm contacts. Tell them how to reach you and when you pick up.
- **Later, consider part-time help.** A few paid hours a week of someone answering calls keeps the human touch without interrupting your repairs.

**Two smaller risks to check**

- **Cash flow while the regulars convert.** £3,500 is spent, so know how many weeks you can cover fuel and parts if bookings start slowly.
- **Spare capacity.** You're one person, so illness, a van breakdown or a big job means no income that day. A small buffer fund matters.

The rest of the plan is strong: real skill, insurance done, equipment owned, and a ready-made customer base most new businesses would envy. The booking policy is the part most likely to quietly leak customers. It's a fixable problem, not a fatal one.

The weakest point is the phone-only booking, and it clashes with how you'll work.

**The problem:** You'll be alone, hands in a bike from 8 to 6, so you'll miss most calls. Someone who rings and gets voicemail will often try the next mobile mechanic rather than wait, and you'll rarely know it happened. Answering mid-job also means stopping work, with greasy hands, and giving the caller half your attention, which undercuts the "real person" experience you want. Many people, especially under 40, also won't phone for a routine booking, so you'd lose some customers before they ever reach you.

**What's safe:** Your 300 inherited regulars already trust you, and many will happily call. Your first months are probably fine. The risk is growth beyond that list, and the strain of being on call all day.

**Ways to keep the human element without the bottleneck:**
- **Set call windows.** Say "I answer calls 8-8:30am, 12-12:30pm and 6-7pm" and put it on the van, voicemail and cards. Customers accept this if it's clear.
- **Return voicemails quickly**, within a couple of hours, with a short, friendly message that sets the expectation.
- **Allow text or WhatsApp as a way to *request* a call.** You're still speaking to everyone, but they don't need you to pick up live.
- **Consider a simple "request a callback" page** or a Google Business Profile with your number. It's not an app or an online booking system, and it's how new customers will find you.
- **If revenue justifies it,** use a part-time virtual receptionist or answering service.

Keep the principle that every customer talks to you, but separate that from needing to answer every call live.

Two smaller things to check: your pricing covers travel time between jobs (it's easy to underprice), and you have a plan for sick days or van breakdowns, since you're a single point of failure.

Your 300 inherited regulars will probably call anyway, but new customers, who are what you need to grow beyond that base, are the ones you'll lose.

The "real person" idea is sound. The mistake is tying it to one channel that you can't staff during working hours. Keep the personal touch but remove the bottleneck: a simple booking page or text-to-book option that you answer personally, with a fast callback promise, such as ringing back within two hours at set times. You could also keep phone as the main route and just add a basic web presence so people can find you and request a slot.

Everything else you've described is strong: the skills, van, insurance and ready-made customer base. This is the one decision that can quietly cap your income, and it's cheap to fix before it does.
